subject: humanities
passage: Until the early 1950s, most jazz recordings were issued on 78-rpm discs, which held only about three minutes of music per side, so musicians often had to trim their performances to fit. Once the long-playing record, or LP, became common, recorded performances grew much longer. Musicologist Rafael Oyelaran, who timed the sections of hundreds of studio recordings, argues that the added length was not distributed evenly across a performance: musicians devoted nearly all of the new time to improvised solos, while the written themes that open and close a piece remained about as long as they had been.

data.title: Average Length of Sections in Studio Jazz Recordings (minutes)

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oyelaran's argument?

choices.A: The average track recorded in 1955–1959 was more than twice as long as the average track recorded in 1945–1949.
choices.B: Of the 4.4 minutes added to the average track between 1945–1949 and 1955–1959, solos accounted for 4.2.
choices.C: In every period shown, musicians spent more time on improvised solos than they did on theme statements.
choices.D: Solos took up a larger share of the average track in 1945–1949 than they did in 1955–1959.

explanation.why: Oyelaran accepts that tracks got longer; his claim is about where the added time went: almost all of it to solos, with themes nearly unchanged. Support must compare the growth of the solo and theme columns with the growth of the whole track. From 1945–1949 to 1955–1959, tracks grew by 7.4 − 3.0 = 4.4 minutes, solos by 6.1 − 1.9 = 4.2 minutes, and themes by only 0.2 minutes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that tracks got longer, which the text already accepts, not which sections absorbed the added time.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows that nearly all of the added time went to solos, leaving theme statements almost unchanged.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but solos could outweigh themes in every period even if both had grown by similar amounts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Solos made up about 63% of a track (1.9 of 3.0 minutes) in 1945–1949 but about 82% (6.1 of 7.4) in 1955–1959, so this reverses the table.
